title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: He could not tell whether it was late or early. The candles had all burned down. Dolly had just been in the study and had suggested that the doctor lie down. Levin sat listening to the doctor's stories about a quack mesmerist and staring at the ash on his cigarette. There had been a stretch of calm, and he had sunk into a kind of blankness. He had completely forgotten what was going on right now. He was hearing the doctor's chatter and following it. Suddenly an unearthly shriek came through. The shriek was so awful that Levin did not even jump up; he held his breath and looked at the doctor with terrified questioning eyes. The doctor cocked his head, listened, and gave an approving smile. Everything was so extraordinary that nothing struck Levin as strange anymore. "I suppose that's how it has to be," he thought, and stayed where he was. Whose scream was that? He jumped up, ran on tiptoe to the bedroom, edged around Lizaveta Petrovna and the princess, and took his place at Kitty's pillow. The scream had stopped, but something had changed. What it was he didn't see and didn't take in, and he had no wish to see or take it in. But he could read it on Lizaveta Petrovna's face. Her face was stern and pale, still as resolute as ever, though her jaw was twitching and her eyes were fixed on Kitty. Kitty's swollen, anguished face, a lock of hair stuck to her damp forehead, was turned to him, searching for his eyes. Her raised hands reached for his. Clutching his cold hands in her hot, wet ones, she began pressing them to her face.
"Don't go, don't go! I'm not afraid, I'm not afraid!" she said quickly. "Mamma, take my earrings. They're bothering me. You're not afraid? Quick, quick, Lizaveta Petrovna...."
She spoke fast, very fast, and tried to smile. But suddenly her face contorted and she pushed him away.
"Oh, this is horrible! I'm dying, I'm dying! Go away!" she shrieked, and again that unearthly scream tore out of her.
Levin clutched his head and ran out of the room.
"It's nothing, it's nothing, it's all fine," Dolly called after him.

But they could say what they liked — he knew now that it was over. He stood in the next room, his head leaning against the doorpost, and listened to shrieks and howls of a kind he had never heard before, and he knew that what had been Kitty was making these sounds. He had long since stopped wanting the child. By now he hated this child. He did not even want her to survive anymore. All he wanted was for this terrible agony to end.
"Doctor! What is it? What is it? My God!" he said, grabbing at the doctor's hand as he came up.
"It's the end," the doctor said. And the doctor's face was so grave as he said it that Levin took _the end_ to mean her death.

Out of his mind, he ran into the bedroom. The first thing he saw was Lizaveta Petrovna's face. It was even more frowning and stern. Kitty's face he could not even recognize. In its place was something fearful in its strained distortion and in the sounds coming out of it. He sank down with his head on the wooden frame of the bed, feeling that his heart was bursting. The awful scream went on and on, and grew worse, and just when it seemed to have hit the absolute outer limit of horror, it stopped. Levin could not believe his ears, but there was no doubt: the scream had stopped, and he could hear a hushed bustle, hurried breathing, and her voice — gasping, alive, tender, blissful — saying softly, "It's over!"
He lifted his head. Her hands lay exhausted on the quilt; she looked extraordinarily lovely and serene; she looked at him in silence and tried to smile, and couldn't.

And suddenly, out of the mysterious and dreadful far-off world he had been living in for the last twenty-two hours, Levin felt himself thrown, in one instant, back into the ordinary everyday world — though now lit up with such a blaze of happiness that he could not bear it. The taut strings snapped; sobs and tears of joy he had never expected rose up with such force that his whole body shook, and for a long time they kept him from speaking.

Dropping to his knees by the bed, he held his wife's hand to his lips and kissed it, and her hand, with a weak movement of the fingers, answered his kiss. And meanwhile, there at the foot of the bed, in the practiced hands of Lizaveta Petrovna, like a flickering flame in a lamp, lay the life of a human being who had never existed before, and who would now, with the same right and the same significance to itself, live and create after its own kind.
"Alive! alive! And a boy too! Don't worry!" Levin heard Lizaveta Petrovna saying, as she slapped the baby's back with a shaking hand.
"Mamma, is it true?" came Kitty's voice.

The princess's sobs were all the answer she could give. And in the middle of the silence came, in unmistakable reply to the mother's question, a voice unlike any of the hushed voices in the room. It was the bold, clamorous, self-assertive squall of the new human being who had so inexplicably arrived.

If Levin had been told before this that Kitty was dead, and that he had died with her, and that their children were angels, and that God was standing in front of him, none of it would have surprised him. But now, coming back into the world of the actual, he had to make a real mental effort to take in that she was alive and well, and that this creature wailing so desperately was his son. Kitty was alive, her agony was over. And he was unspeakably happy. That he understood; he was completely happy in that. But the baby? Where from, why, who was he?... He could not get used to the idea. It felt like something extra, something superfluous, something he couldn't acclimatize himself to.
